name: Bartholomew
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: A name in every list of the Twelve; perhaps the Nathanael of John’s Gospel.
story: One of the Twelve, known in Scripture only by his name in the lists of the apostles.

entries.title: No home given; Nathanael of Cana
entries.text: Scripture gives no home for Bartholomew. Nathanael was “of Cana in Galilee” (John 21:2).

entries.title: “Son of Talmai”
entries.text: The name Bartholomew means “son of Talmai” (or Tholmai). Fenlon (1907) notes that it may have been his own name, or a family name added to tell him apart.

entries.title: In the upper room
entries.text: He is named seventh among the Eleven in the upper room (Acts 1:13). Acts never names him again.

entries.title: Eusebius, Church History 5.10.3, reporting Pantaenus’s journey
entries.text: Pantaenus “is said to have gone to India. It is reported that … he found the Gospel according to Matthew”, for “Bartholomew, one of the apostles, had preached to them, and left with them the writing of Matthew in the Hebrew language”.

entries.title: J. F. Fenlon, Catholic Encyclopedia
entries.text: “No mention of St. Bartholomew occurs in ecclesiastical literature before Eusebius.” Other traditions send him to Mesopotamia, Persia, Egypt, Armenia, Lycaonia, Phrygia and the Black Sea coast.

entries.title: Later traditions, as summarised by J. F. Fenlon
entries.text: He died at Albanopolis in Armenia: “according to some, he was beheaded, according to others, flayed alive and crucified, head downward”. Fenlon calls the manner of death “equally uncertain”.

items.q: Is Bartholomew the same man as Nathanael?
items.full: Is Bartholomew the same man as Nathanael?

argument.text: Its opening list of apostles names Bartholomew and Nathanael as two men. The same list also names Peter and Cephas as two.

views.label: Nathanael was not one of the Twelve

argument.text: Augustine reasons that Nathanael “was learned and skilled in the law and for that reason was the Lord unwilling to place him among His disciples”, because he chose unlearned men.

views.label: The same man: Nathanael, son of Talmai
views.holders: Ishodad of Merv (about 850); generally held from the 9th century on (Kerr, 1915); reasons set out by Fenlon (1907)

argument.text: John never uses the name Bartholomew and the other Gospels never use Nathanael; the Gospel lists pair Bartholomew with Philip, who brought Nathanael; Nathanael was among disciples with apostles in John 21:2. Fenlon calls the case “ingenious and pretty strong”, with the weak link that Nathanael “may have been another personage”.

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: Bartholomew appears only in the four lists of the Twelve. Nathanael appears only in John’s Gospel (John 1:45–51; 21:2), which never uses the name Bartholomew.

items.q: Why does Bartholomew stand beside Philip?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Bartholomew is named straight after Philip; in Acts 1:13 Thomas comes between them. In John, Philip is the one who brings Nathanael to Jesus (John 1:45).

items.q: Who first made the two one man?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The earliest writer found who equates the two is Ishodad of Merv (about 850): “Bartholomew is perhaps Nathanael”, and “It is handed down that Nathanael, that is to say, Bar Toulmi, was well acquainted with the Scriptures”. This page shows both records and treats the identification as a view.
